name: Abigail
charge: Keeping David from shedding blood and avenging himself with his own hand
summary: Her husband Nabal railed on David's men; David strapped on his sword to kill every male of the house by morning. Abigail met him on the road with two hundred loaves and a speech that is one of the wisest in scripture, and turned him back. Ten days later the Lord smote Nabal, and David sent for her.
offense: Abigail heard from a servant what Nabal had done and what David's men had done for the household. The men had protected the shepherds; Nabal had railed upon their messengers; now destruction threatened the house (1 Samuel 25:14-17). She did not make loyalty to her husband mean agreement with his folly. She acted to preserve the household he had placed in danger. She prepared substantial provision and went to meet David without first telling Nabal. David had already armed his men and sworn to leave no male of the house alive (1 Samuel 25:18-22). Her haste addressed a danger that could not wait for the husband described as unwilling to hear reason. The food answered the need; her speech addressed the wrath. She humbled herself, took the burden of pleading upon herself, and named Nabal's folly without disguising it. Then she directed David toward the future the Lord had promised him. When he ruled Israel, he should not carry the grief of causeless bloodshed or self-avenging violence (1 Samuel 25:23-31). She appealed to his calling against the conduct his anger was about to produce. Wise counsel did not flatter the armed man; it stopped him. Proverbs 14:1 says that a wise woman builds her house. Abigail's conduct protected more than its possessions. It preserved lives and called the approaching king back to the fear of the Lord. She neither approved Nabal's railing nor answered it by delivering him to David's sword.
judgment: David blessed the Lord who sent her, blessed her advice, and acknowledged that she had kept him from shedding blood and avenging himself. He accepted the provision and sent her home in peace (1 Samuel 25:32-35). Her counsel succeeded because he received correction while there was still time to turn from the act. At home she again governed the moment of speaking. Nabal was drunk, so she waited until morning. After he heard what had happened, he became as a stone, and about ten days later the Lord smote him (1 Samuel 25:36-38). The household was spared David's intended slaughter; Nabal's own judgment remained with the Lord. David then sought Abigail as his wife, and she answered with the same humility that had marked her appeal (1 Samuel 25:39-42). The blessing follows a woman of understanding who brought provision, spoke truth, and preserved another from sin. Her wisdom was not merely knowledge of what was right. It was the ability to bring that knowledge to bear before blood was shed.

entries.commentary: Samuel died, and all the Israelites gathered together and lamented him and buried him in his house at Ramah; and David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran. There was a very great man in Maon whose possessions were in Carmel, three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, shearing his sheep in Carmel. His name was Nabal, and his wife was Abigail, a woman of good understanding and of a beautiful countenance; but the man was churlish and evil in his doings, and he was of the house of Caleb.

David heard in the wilderness that Nabal did shear his sheep and sent ten young men to greet him in peace: peace be to thee, to thine house, and to all that thou hast. The request was righteous: thy shepherds were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them all the while they were in Carmel; ask thy young men and they will shew thee. We come in a good day; give whatsoever cometh to thine hand unto thy servants and to thy son David.

Nabal answered, Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master. He was talking much smack, as if he did not even know who David was, and refused to give of his bread, his water, and his flesh to men he knew not. When his young men told David, he said, Gird ye on every man his sword; about four hundred men went up after David, and two hundred abode by the stuff.

One of the young men told Abigail: David sent messengers out of the wilderness to salute our master, and he railed on them. But the men were very good unto us; we were not hurt, neither missed we any thing as long as we were conversant with them; they were a wall unto us both by night and day while we were keeping the sheep. David's men had been giving Nabal's shepherds protection from their enemies. Evil is determined against our master and against all his household, for he is such a son of Belial that a man cannot speak to him. Some of us know people like that: you cannot talk to them, they will not reason with you. Consider that Nabal was rich, a very wealthy man, and a lot of times what comes with that is an arrogant spirit.

Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, clusters of raisins, and cakes of figs, laid them on asses, and sent her servants on before her; but she told not her husband Nabal. David had said, Surely in vain have I kept all that this fellow hath in the wilderness; he hath requited me evil for good. He swore to leave Nabal none by the morning light of any that pisseth against the wall; David was coming with intent to destroy the men of that house.

When Abigail saw David she hasted, lighted off the ass, fell at his feet, and said, Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be. She was not the one who did anything wrong, but she took that iniquity upon herself; she was being that pillar of her house, using wisdom to protect it, for the scripture says she was a woman of good understanding. She did not turn her lord over to be destroyed, as some women today would be ready to do; instead she pleaded, Let not my lord regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. She had not seen the young men David sent, or she would have stepped in then to protect their house.

Abigail said, The Lord hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood and from avenging thyself with thine own hand; now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal. She asked, Forgive the trespass of thine handmaid; it was Nabal who was out of the spirit, but again that chaste conversation, stepping up for her household. The soul of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord thy God, and the souls of thine enemies, them shall he sling out as out of the middle of a sling. When the Lord shall have appointed thee ruler over Israel, this shall be no grief unto thee, that thou hast shed blood causeless or that my lord hath avenged himself; then remember thine handmaid.

David said, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me, and blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood and from avenging myself with mine own hand. David received of her hand that which she had brought him and said, Go up in peace to thine house; see, I have hearkened to thy voice and have accepted thy person.

Abigail came home and Nabal held a feast in his house like the feast of a king, and his heart was merry within him, for he was very drunken; so she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light. In the morning, when the wine was gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. Remember he had railed, Who is David? but when he sobered up and heard that the coming king had come down to destroy everybody in his house, his heart died within him. About ten days after, the Lord smote Nabal, that he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, Blessed be the Lord, that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and hath kept his servant from evil: for the Lord hath returned the wickedness of Nabal upon his own head. Then David sent and communed with Abigail, to take her to him to wife. Abigail bowed herself on her face to the earth and said, Behold, let thine handmaid be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord, and she arose and washed the feet of the servants who delivered the good tidings; that is a very humble act. She was probably very joyous and glad to go: a woman living with a man who is hard to deal with, who will not listen, will not take advice, arrogant, maybe verbally abusive, was relieved of that thing when Nabal died, and she hasted and arose with five damsels of hers and became David's wife.
David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and they were also both of them his wives; but Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Phalti the son of Laish, which was of Gallim.

There was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David, but David waxed stronger and stronger and the house of Saul weaker and weaker. Each had those that followed him, but the Most High increased David because he had been anointed to be the next king over Israel.

Sons were born to David in Hebron: the firstborn Amnon of Ahinoam, Chileab of Abigail, Absalom the son of Maachah the daughter of the king of Geshur, Adonijah the son of Haggith, Shephatiah of Abital, and Ithream of Eglah his wife. Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul. When Ishbosheth charged him over Rizpah, Saul's concubine, Abner was very wroth, saying he had shown kindness to the house of Saul and not delivered them to David, and now was charged with a fault concerning this woman. Abner swore to do to himself and more, to translate the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba. Ishbosheth could not answer him a word, because he feared him. Abner was through with Ishbosheth and turned to go with David and the Lord.

Abner sent messengers to David offering to bring all Israel to him. David agreed to make a league, but required that Michal, Saul's daughter, first be brought to him, and he sent to Ishbosheth to deliver his wife whom he had espoused for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines. Michal was taken from her husband Phaltiel, who went weeping behind her until Abner told him to return. David was taking back what was his as the king before the Lord. Abner spoke with the elders of Israel and with Benjamin, reminding them they had sought David in times past, and that the Lord had said by the hand of David He would save Israel out of the hand of the Philistines and all their enemies. Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David made them a feast, and Abner went in peace to gather all Israel to David.

Joab returned from pursuing a troop and heard that Abner had come and been sent away in peace. Joab came to the king and said Abner had come to deceive him and to know his going out and coming in; he did not trust Abner, and there was already blood between them, for Abner had killed Asahel his brother. Joab, without David's knowledge, sent messengers after Abner and brought him back to Hebron, took him aside in the gate to speak quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. It was payback; Joab's blood was burning for revenge. Abner was unwise to return to that place, knowing what Joab would do, but it was of the Lord.

When David heard it, he declared himself and his kingdom guiltless before the Lord forever from the blood of Abner, and laid it on the head of Joab and all his father's house. He commanded Joab and all the people to rend their clothes and gird with sackcloth and mourn before Abner, and the king himself followed the coffin. David wept at the grave and lamented over Abner in the spirit, another eulogy and prophecy: Abner died as a fool dieth, his hands not bound nor his feet in fetters, but he fell as a man falleth before wicked men. All the people wept again and took notice, and David swore not to taste bread till the sun went down, and it pleased the people; whatsoever the king did pleased them, for David was in the right spirit and the Lord was dealing with the nation. David said he was weak that day though anointed king, and that the sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him, ruthless men he could not bring under; but the Lord would reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness. That payback came later through Solomon concerning Joab.
